items.title: Warm temperatures delay opening of ice rink at Celebration Square in Mississauga
items.summary: Mild temperatures have once again spoiled plans for people who’ve wanted to lace up their skates and get on the ice at Celebration Square in Mississauga’s downtown core. The city’s biggest outdoor skating rink usually opens for the late fall/winter season at the same time the City of Mississauga hosts its annual Christmas tree lighting ceremony at the downtown venue. The tree-lighting festivities, along with the annual Santa Claus parade, went ahead as scheduled last Saturday in the City Centre. However, warmer-than-usual temperartures prevented the ice rink from being available. “We usually start making ice in mid-November so the rink can open around the annual tree lighting ceremony. This year, this wasn’t possible due to mild temperatures,” City of Mississauga spokesperson Irene McCutcheon told INSAUGA Canada on Thursday. “Staff are working hard to get the Celebration Square rink ready, with a target opening date of Dec. 4, weather permitting. Ultimately, the weather will determine when the ice is ready. ” Warmer-than-normal temperatures back in March also disappointed many avid skaters looking to do laps on the Celebration Square ice rink at that time. The attraction closed earlier than usual, ending its seasonal run on March 7, well before March break. Mississauga officials said earlier this month that a potentially historic El Niño is expected to bring milder temperatures to southern Ontario this fall and winter. It’s expected to impact the city in several ways. City officials and many residents are also waiting for colder temperatures to set in so they can ensure a Canadian winter tradition returns to as many Mississauga neighbourhoods as possible in the coming months.

items.title: Mississauga Chinese Centre approved for heritage designation despite opposition
items.summary: The Mississauga Chinese Centre was approved for a heritage designation despite opposition from the plaza’s owner. The centre, located at 888 Dundas St. , was developed by Hong Kong investors in the 1980s. It features replica landmarks from China, including the “nine-dragon wall” and a large entry gate with Chinese-inspired elements, a report to Mississauga’s Heritage Advisory Committee states. The city added the property to the Heritage Register in 1989, but it was considered for a heritage designation at the Heritage Advisory Committee on Nov. 24. Speaking on behalf of the current owner, lawyer Rodney Gill told the committee the Mississauga Chinese Centre doesn’t meet the criteria for a designation. Through a translator, the owner said the designation will delay needed repairs and leave business owners with more expensive renovations. He “strongly” opposed the designation. Gill said the staff report was completed about a year ago, and there have been several changes since then. Statues have been removed, the garden and a building known as the fortress have been altered and no longer have the same appearance, Gill said.

items.title: 8 tower cranes doing the heavy lifting to build Canada’s biggest hospital in Mississauga
items.summary: 9-billion “state-of-the-art” hospital expected to be the biggest in Canada when completed. The tallest of the cranes rises up 146 metres, or about one-quarter the height of the CN Tower in Toronto. The heavy construction equipment working on The Queensway West/Hurontario Street megaproject can produce a great deal of noise on occasion. That’s why project leaders say they’ve taken steps to keep a lid — as much as possible, anyway — on the commotion in order to lessen the impact on residents in the surrounding neighbourhoods. “We know construction noise can be disruptive for our neighbours. We’re taking steps to reduce it, including a sound wall by the truck waiting area, quieter equipment and scheduling higher-impact work during the day wherever possible,” Trillium Health Partners said this week in its latest community update. “With eight tower cranes on site, (residents) may still hear crane horns at times. Crane operators sound a horn to warn workers below when a load is being lifted overhead. ” Trillium Health Partners is the health-care network that oversees Mississauga and Credit Valley hospitals in Mississauga in addition to Queensway Health Centre in Etobicoke, just steps east of the city. Expected to be the biggest hospital in Canada when it opens to patients in 2034, The Peter Gilgan Mississauga Hospital will rise up 22 storeys on the same site as the current Mississauga Hospital. 8 million sq. ft. in size and will house within it the Shah Family Hospital for Women and Children, to be the first such medical facility in Ontario.

items.title: 5 home invasions in Mississauga, Brampton and Toronto lead to 2 arrests
items.summary: Last Updated November 26, 2026 at 4:14 pm Two people face numerous charges in the wake of a major investigation into five home invasions in Mississauga, Brampton and Toronto in which the culprits targeted luxury vehicles, police say. Investigators believe one of the suspects facing charges was also involved in two tow truck arsons in Brampton, Peel Regional Police said on Thursday. ” In each case, the culprits “forcibly entered residences in the early morning hours and demanded vehicle keys from occupants,” police said, adding several luxury vehicles, including BMW and Mercedes models, were either stolen or targeted during the home invasions. “Fortunately, none of the victims were physically injured,” police noted. Police subsequently launched an investigation dubbed Project Twilight, a coordinated probe involving members of Peel’s Central Robbery Bureau and “other specialized units” including officers with the Toronto Police Hold-Up Squad. Detectives arrested two suspects on June 8, police said this week, adding two loaded illegal firearms, ammunition and approximately 76 grams of suspected fentanyl were recovered at the same time.

items.title: Seminar teaches real-world financial skills to students in Mississauga and Brampton
items.summary: A new series of seminars will teach Peel District School Board students financial skills to help them manage their finances after graduation. The partnership between the Peel District School Board and the Bank of Canada Museum launched on Thursday, bringing some 250 students from Grades 10 to 12 together for workshops with Bank of Canada staff. From the role of Canada’s central bank and interest rate decisions to economic data and trends and financial literacy, the year-long program will give students first-hand learning about career pathways in economics, research, financial markets, public service and policy-making, the PDSB says. ” Updated curriculum requirements for financial literacy were set to take effect at the beginning of this school year with a mandatory test. Students must achieve a score of 70 per cent or higher on financial literacy modules, and the assessment will account for 5 per cent of the final grade in the Grade 10 Career Studies course. “Once the requirement has been successfully completed, it will be noted on the student’s Ontario Student Transcript,” the PDSB says. The requirement builds on financial literacy learning introduced throughout Grades 1 to 9 and complements the learning in the Grade 10 Career Studies curriculum, the board says. The province has said that students will learn home economics such as managing a household budget, and will need to score at least 70 per cent on a financial literacy test in order to graduate.

items.title: Ontario to Require Licences and Insurance for Motorcycle-Style E-Bikes Next May
items.summary: According to insauga.com, Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced that drivers of motorcycle-style e-bikes will need a driver's licence, registration and insurance to operate on provincial roads starting next May. Sarkaria said vehicles that look like e-bikes but function more like motorcycles pose serious risks to pedestrians, cyclists, riders and drivers. Under the new definition, a true e-bike must have a bicycle-style frame, operable pedals and a motor-assisted top speed of 32 km/h, with anything faster banned from bike lanes and subject to the new licensing rules. The province said penalties will include fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment. Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo welcomed the change, saying residents have called for stronger e-bike safety measures for years as the city grapples with danger on its streets from some riders.

items.title: 2 arrested after investigation into series of home invasions across GTA: Peel police
items.summary: Two people have been charged as the result of an investigation into an alleged spree of home invasions, Peel Regional Police announced Thursday. Multiple charges related to the robberies, as well as illegal firearms, drugs and possession of child sexual abuse material have been laid, and police expect more arrests to come.

items.title: Port Credit's 130-Year-Old United Church Could Become City-Owned Event Venue
items.summary: According to insauga.com, the City of Mississauga is in the process of buying a more than 130-year-old United Church property at 151 Lakeshore Rd. W. in Port Credit, which has been listed for sale for nearly six months. Then-Mayor Carolyn Parrish announced in July that the city planned to turn the building into an event venue and a permanent home for the Canada Virtuoso Ensemble. The church, most recently known as Christ First United Church, amalgamated with the Clarkson Christ First United Church on Mazo Crescent in 2019 and moved its regular services there the same year. A Spanish-language congregation currently holds services in the Port Credit building on typical Sundays, according to a church spokesperson. The congregation is also planning a Candlelight Service at the Port Credit church in December, the spokesperson said.

items.title: UTM Intern's New Series Traces Mississauga's Ties to Japanese Canadian Internment
items.summary: According to Modern Mississauga Media, a new four-part series is tracing the connections between Mississauga and the internment of Japanese Canadians during the Second World War. The series, titled A Path to Mississauga, was researched and written by Darrion Singh, a University of Toronto Mississauga graduate who completed a Historical Studies internship with Heritage Mississauga from September 2025 to March 2026. Singh's project revisits how Canada declared war on Japan on Dec. 7, 1941, after the attack on Pearl Harbor, and how Ottawa later invoked the War Measures Act to expel Japanese Canadians from British Columbia by early 1942. The outlet reports Singh credits Heritage Mississauga and University of Toronto Mississauga staff for guiding the internship. The series will explore how Japanese Canadians remember this history and its ties to the Mississauga area, Singh says.
